outcomes.text: Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of the conventions of a wide range of written textual forms (suggested examples, not prescribed: advertisements, brochures, leaflets, editorials, news stories, articles, reviews, blogs, investigative journalism, letters, podcasts, (auto)biographies, travel writing, diaries, essays, scripted speech, narrative writing, and descriptive writing).

Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of the linguistic elements and literary features of texts (suggested examples, not prescribed: parts of speech / word classes, vocabulary, figurative language, phonology, morphology, rhetorical devices, voice, aspect, tense, modality, narrative perspective, word ordering and sentence structure, paragraph- and text-level structure, formality/informality of tone, pragmatics).
Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of the significance of audience in both the design and reception of texts.
Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of the ways in which genre, purpose and context contribute to the meaning of texts.
Demonstrate the skill of reading a range of unseen texts.
Demonstrate the skill of analysing the ways in which linguistic elements come together in a text to create meaning.
Demonstrate the skill of recognising different nonfiction textual forms and their conventions.
Demonstrate the skill of writing analytically about the effects produced by a range of linguistic elements and literary features.
Demonstrate the skill of integrating individual analytical points into broader overall responses to texts.
Demonstrate the skill of selecting and interpreting words and phrases from a text with care and precision.
Demonstrate the skill of recognising and commenting on the overall style of a text, and exemplifying this through specific instances of language analysis.
Demonstrate the skill of using quotations and evidence, with judgement, to produce precise, meaningful commentaries.
Demonstrate the skill of using appropriate language to link quotations and evidence with explanatory comments.
Demonstrate the skill of integrating quotations and evidence into a cohesive argument.
Demonstrate the skill of writing short, directed pieces in response to a text.
Demonstrate the skill of writing in the same style as another text.
Demonstrate the skill of writing in a different style from a text at the same time as re-using the content/material.
Demonstrate the skill of comparing the style and linguistic elements of their own writing with those of a given text.

subtopics.title: Textual forms and linguistic features for writing

outcomes.text: Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of the conventions of a wide range of written textual forms (suggested examples, not prescribed: advertisements, brochures, leaflets, editorials, news stories, articles, reviews, blogs, investigative journalism, letters, podcasts, (auto)biographies, travel writing, diaries, essays, scripted speech, narrative writing, and descriptive writing).

Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of the linguistic elements and literary features of texts (suggested examples, not prescribed: parts of speech / word classes, vocabulary, figurative language, phonology, morphology, rhetorical devices, voice, aspect, tense, modality, narrative perspective, word ordering and sentence structure, paragraph- and text-level structure, formality/informality of tone, pragmatics).
Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of the significance of audience in both the design and reception of texts.
Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of the ways in which genre, purpose and context contribute to the meaning of texts.
Demonstrate the skill of writing for a specified audience and purpose, to fulfil the brief provided.

Demonstrate the skill of producing an appropriate structure for longer pieces of writing (suggested examples, not prescribed: Freytag’s Pyramid in imaginative writing; dialectical structure in discursive writing; introductory, summary and evaluative sections in review writing).

Demonstrate the skill of organising writing to achieve specific effects (suggested examples, not prescribed: withholding key information in imaginative writing; juxtaposing counterarguments in discursive writing; evidentiary logic in critical writing).
Demonstrate the skill of structuring paragraphs (suggested examples, not prescribed: topic sentences, connectives, internal coherence, discourse markers).

Demonstrate the skill of using a range of appropriate linguistic elements and literary features (suggested examples, not prescribed: imagery in descriptive writing; rhetorical devices in argumentative writing; evaluative lexis in critical writing).
Demonstrate the skill of expressing ideas accurately and clearly at both sentence and word level.
Demonstrate the skill of reflecting upon and evaluating the qualities of their own writing, including aspects relating to its purpose, form and audience.

Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of the chronology and essential features of the development of the English language from Early Modern English to Contemporary English (suggested examples, not prescribed: graphology, orthography, phonology, morphology, syntax, lexis, semantics, pragmatics, grammar).

Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of concepts and terminology related to language change (suggested examples, not prescribed: etymology, derivation, inflection, telescoping, coalescence, acronym, conversion, compounding, backformation, blending, borrowing, amelioration, pejoration, broadening, narrowing).

Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of theories and theorists of language change (suggested examples, not prescribed: random fluctuation theory, cultural transmission theory, theory of lexical gaps, substratum theory, functional theory, tree and wave models).

Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of n-gram graphs representing changes in language use over time (suggested examples, not prescribed: comparisons of related words, parts of speech, inflections, collocations).
Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of word tables derived from corpus data (suggested examples, not prescribed: collocate lists, synonym lists).
Demonstrate the skill of researching in the field of language change.
Demonstrate the skill of analysing unseen texts as exemplars of certain aspects of language change.
Demonstrate the skill of interpreting and analysing n-gram graphs and corpus data relating to language change.
Demonstrate the skill of contextualising findings alongside relevant theories and concepts relating to language change.
Demonstrate the skill of synthesising their responses to a range of language data into a coherent analytical essay.

subtopics.title: Child language acquisition: knowledge and understanding

outcomes.text: Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of the main stages of early development (0–8 years) in child language acquisition (suggested examples, not prescribed: babbling, holophrastic, telegraphic and post-telegraphic stages).

Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of the different functions of children’s language (suggested examples, not prescribed: instrumental, regulatory, interactional, personal, representational, heuristic, imaginative).

Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of theories and theorists of child language acquisition (suggested examples, not prescribed: imitation and reinforcement theory, language acquisition device, language acquisition support system, cognitive development theory, child-directed or caretaker speech).

Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of the conventions and features of unscripted conversation and spoken language transcripts (suggested examples, not prescribed: notation for pauses, overlaps, stress, intonation and phonemic features).

subtopics.title: Child language acquisition: skills and techniques

outcomes.text: Demonstrate the skill of researching in the field of child language acquisition.
Demonstrate the skill of analysing spoken language transcripts as exemplars of certain aspects of child language acquisition.
Demonstrate the skill of interpreting and analysing instances of conversation involving children aged 0 to 8 years.
Demonstrate the skill of contextualising findings alongside relevant theories and concepts relating to child language acquisition.
Demonstrate the skill of synthesising these theoretical considerations into a coherent analytical essay.

topics.title: Section A: English in the world

subtopics.title: English in the world: knowledge and understanding

outcomes.text: Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of theories, theorists and studies relating to the historical development of English as a ‘global’ language (suggested examples, not prescribed: colonialism, cultural influence and effects, concentric circles model, multilingualism, the future of English).

Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of theories, theorists and studies relating to varieties of English (suggested examples, not prescribed: standard and nonstandard ‘Englishes’, creolisation, sociolect continuum, official and unofficial attitudes and policies).

Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of theories, theorists and studies relating to relevant ethical considerations (suggested examples, not prescribed: language shift and death, cultural imperialism, equality of opportunity, global cooperation).

subtopics.title: English in the world: skills and techniques

outcomes.text: Demonstrate the skill of reading and demonstrating critical understanding of unseen texts relating to ‘English in the world’.
Demonstrate the skill of selecting and analysing pertinent ideas and examples from the texts.
Demonstrate the skill of relating these ideas and examples to theories, theorists and studies from their wider research in the relevant topic area.
Demonstrate the skill of synthesising these considerations into a coherent analytical essay.

topics.title: Section B: Language and the self

subtopics.title: Language and the self: knowledge and understanding

outcomes.text: Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of theories, theorists and studies relating to innateness and learning (suggested examples, not prescribed: behaviourism, innatism, nativism, empiricism).

Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of theories, theorists and studies relating to the relationship between language and thought (suggested examples, not prescribed: linguistic relativity and determinism, universalism, language of thought hypothesis).

Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of theories, theorists and studies relating to the relationship between language and social identity (suggested examples, not prescribed: speech communities, prestige, idiolect, dialect, sociolect, genderlect, variation, standard and nonstandard features, inclusion and exclusion, speech sounds and accents).

subtopics.title: Language and the self: skills and techniques

outcomes.text: Demonstrate the skill of reading and demonstrating critical understanding of unseen texts relating to ‘Language and the self’.
Demonstrate the skill of selecting and analysing pertinent ideas and examples from the texts.
Demonstrate the skill of relating these ideas and examples to theories, theorists and studies from their wider research in the relevant topic area.
Demonstrate the skill of synthesising these considerations into a coherent analytical essay.
